books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — The Progressive Movement
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

source: original; documents drawn from public-domain sources and book-grounded paraphrases
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Progressive movement changed the role of the federal government in American life from 1900 to 1920.

documents.title: Roosevelt and the coal strike
documents.source: President Theodore Roosevelt's handling of the anthracite coal strike, 1902. Paraphrased from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20.
documents.text: In 1902, anthracite coal miners went on strike, and President Roosevelt called representatives of both management and labor to the White House. He threatened to take over the mines if the owners would not negotiate in good faith. The miners received a 10 percent wage increase, but not union recognition. Roosevelt called the settlement a 'Square Deal' for both sides.
documents.sourcing: Roosevelt, the president, presenting his own settlement as fair to both sides. A public account of a presidential intervention, meant to show government refereeing capital and labor.

documents.title: The Jungle
documents.source: Upton Sinclair, The Jungle, 1906. Paraphrased; the novel is in the public domain.
documents.text: Sinclair's novel follows a Lithuanian immigrant family through the stockyards of Chicago. It describes meat packed in filthy rooms, workers laboring in dangerous conditions, and diseased animals ground into sausage. Sinclair meant the book as a socialist attack on capitalism, but readers seized on the filth in the packing plants.
documents.sourcing: Sinclair, a socialist novelist writing to expose capitalism. His descriptions of the packing plants, not his socialist message, are what moved readers and lawmakers.

documents.title: Federal Meat Inspection Act
documents.source: Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906. Verbatim excerpt, public domain (abridged).
documents.text: For the purposes hereinbefore set forth the Secretary shall cause to be made, by inspectors appointed for that purpose, an examination and inspection of all cattle, sheep, swine, and goats before they shall be allowed to enter into any slaughtering, packing, or canning establishment... and said inspectors shall have access at all times, by day or night, whether the establishment be operated or not, to every part of said establishment; and said inspectors shall mark, stamp, tag, or label as 'Inspected and passed' all such products found to be not adulterated.
documents.sourcing: Congress writing a federal law: inspectors appointed by the Secretary of Agriculture, with access to every part of a packing plant, stamping approved products 'Inspected and passed.'

documents.title: Girl working in a cannery
documents.source: Photograph by Lewis Hine, 1911. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Hine, a photographer working for reform groups, presenting one young worker to middle-class readers. A portrait meant to build support for child labor laws.

documents.title: Seventeenth Amendment
documents.source: Seventeenth Amendment to the Constitution, ratified 1913. Verbatim text, public domain.
documents.text: The Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, elected by the people thereof, for six years; and each Senator shall have one vote. The electors in each State shall have the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures.
documents.sourcing: The Constitution itself, as amended: senators now chosen by voters rather than by state legislatures. The amendment's plain language is the reform.

documents.title: Federal Reserve Act
documents.source: Federal Reserve Act, 1913. Paraphrased from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20.
documents.text: The act created a central banking system of twelve regional banks that could lend to commercial banks in their districts. A Federal Reserve Board in Washington oversaw the system and controlled a new paper currency, the Federal Reserve note. The law aimed to give the country a stable yet flexible currency and to end the panics that had shaken the banks.
documents.sourcing: Congress and President Wilson describing a new federal institution. A law written after the Panic of 1907, when a private banker, J. P. Morgan, had to rescue the banks.

documents.title: The color line and the NAACP
documents.source: W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk, 1903 (verbatim, public domain), and the founding of the NAACP, 1909. Paraphrase follows the quotation.
documents.text: 'For the problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line.' Du Bois demanded full political equality and civil rights for Black Americans. In 1909 he helped found the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People to combat racism and advocate equal rights for all.
documents.sourcing: Du Bois, a Black scholar and activist, speaking to a white-dominated reform movement that largely ignored Black Americans. A demand for equality from outside the Progressive mainstream.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the Progressive movement changed the role of the federal government from 1900 to 1920, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the industrialization and urbanization of the Gilded Age, the growth of trusts and political machines, or the Populist revolt of the 1890s.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the changing federal role.
rubric.notEarned: Naming documents without describing their content does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument about the changing federal role.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or describing them without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Hepburn Act, the Sixteenth Amendment, the Clayton Antitrust Act, or the Eighteenth Amendment.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to Progressive reform with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation, such as Roosevelt presenting his own settlement, Sinclair writing as a socialist, or Du Bois speaking from outside the Progressive mainstream.
rubric.notEarned: Naming an author without explaining why the authorship matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change by area, explaining that the federal role grew in business regulation and democracy but not for Black Americans or farm workers, or weighing continuity against change.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Progressive movement changed the federal government from a night watchman into an active referee and regulator: it gained power to break up trusts, inspect food, run a central bank, and answer directly to voters, yet the change was bounded, because the same government left segregation and farm labor largely untouched.
Context: The Gilded Age left the federal government small beside giant trusts, city machines, and unregulated factories, and the Populist revolt of the 1890s had already shown farmers demanding government action.
Evidence: Documents 1-3 show the new referee state: Roosevelt settling the coal strike, Sinclair's novel moving readers, and Congress answering with federal meat inspection. Documents 4-6 show the change reaching children, voters, and banks: Hine's photograph pressing child labor reform, the Seventeenth Amendment making senators answer to voters, and the Federal Reserve Act giving Washington control of credit.
Beyond the documents: The Hepburn Act of 1906 gave the Interstate Commerce Commission power to set railroad rates, the Sixteenth Amendment funded the larger government with an income tax, and the Clayton Antitrust Act of 1914 exempted unions from antitrust prosecution.
Sourcing: Roosevelt presents his own settlement as fair, Sinclair writes as a socialist whose message readers ignored, and Du Bois speaks from outside a movement that largely ignored Black Americans.
Complexity: The federal role grew unevenly. It expanded in business regulation, consumer protection, banking, and democracy, but Document 7 shows its limits: the same era's government resegregated its own offices, and farm workers saw little of the reform energy at all.
